title: A Rapid, Bloody Run of Kings
overview: Israel's northern kingdom goes through murder, a seven day king and civil war before Omri takes power and his son Ahab openly brings in the worship of Baal.

parts.label: Warning against Baasha (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: The prophet Jehu tells King Baasha that because he kept Israel worshiping at Jeroboam's calf shrines, his family will be wiped out like Jeroboam's, their bodies left unburied, a deep disgrace at the time. Verse 7 adds that Baasha is also guilty for destroying Jeroboam's family; many interpreters think this is because, though that fall was foretold, Baasha acted for his own gain.

parts.label: Elah killed, family wiped out (vv. 8-14)
parts.note: Baasha's son Elah was getting drunk at his steward's house while his army was at war, and Zimri, one of his chariot commanders, murdered him. Zimri then killed every male relative and ally of Baasha, which the writer presents as Jehu's warning coming true.

parts.label: Zimri's seven day reign (vv. 15-20)
parts.note: When the army besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon heard the news, they made their general Omri king and marched on the capital, Tirzah. Trapped, Zimri set the palace on fire around himself, and his name later became an insult meaning a traitor (2 Kings 9:31).

parts.label: Civil war and Omri's rule (vv. 21-28)
parts.note: The dates suggest Israel was split for about four years between Tibni and Omri, and the text does not say how Tibni died. Omri built a new capital at Samaria, and Assyrian records later called Israel 'the house of Omri,' yet the Bible gives him only a few verses and judges him harshly.

parts.label: Ahab turns to Baal (vv. 29-33)
parts.note: Ahab married Jezebel, daughter of the king of Sidon, a Phoenician city, and built a temple in Samaria for Baal, a storm and fertility god, plus an Asherah pole, a wooden symbol of a goddess. Earlier northern kings worshiped the LORD through calf images, but Ahab openly backed another god, setting the stage for the Elijah stories that follow.

parts.label: Jericho rebuilt at a cost (v. 34)
parts.note: Joshua had declared that whoever rebuilt Jericho would lose his oldest and youngest sons (Joshua 6:26), and Hiel's two sons died as he built it. Scholars are unsure whether they died naturally or were sacrificed in a building ritual, but the writer presents it as the old curse coming true.

think: When power keeps changing hands through violence, what do you think it would actually take to break the cycle?
